text: Martin Creed, born on 21 October 1968 in Wakefield, England, is a British artist, composer, and performer who lives and works in London. He moved to Glasgow at age 3 when his father, a silversmith, took a teaching position there. Raised in a Quaker household, Creed attended Lenzie Academy and studied art at the Slade School of Art, University College London, from 1986 to 1990. He lived in London except for a period from 2000 to 2004 when he resided in Alicudi, an island off Sicily. Creed won the Turner Prize in 2001 for two exhibitions, Martin Creed Works and Art Now: Martin Creed, held across England during the preceding year. His submission for the Turner Prize show at the Tate Gallery was Work No. 227: The lights going on and off, an empty room where the lights switched on and off every five seconds. The jury praised the work for its audacity, strength, rigour, wit, and sensitivity to the site, despite controversy from visitors who protested by throwing eggs, claiming Creed’s work was not real art and that painting was at risk of extinction. Since 1987, Creed has numbered each of his works, with titles often descriptive, such as Work No. 79: some Blu-tack kneaded, rolled into a ball and depressed against a wall (1993) and Work No. 88: a sheet of A4 paper crumpled into a ball (1995). Work No. 200: Half the air in a given space (1998) is a room filled with half its cubic space in balloons. Work No. 19: An Intrusion And A Protrusion From A Wall, first exhibited at the Slade in 1989, was later replaced in 1990 by Work No. 21 with slightly different content, challenging ideas of reproducibility and authenticity in art. In 2009, he created Work No. 1020: Ballet, a live performance combining music, ballet, words, and film, originally produced by Sadler's Wells and performed in the Lilian Baylis Studio, later staged in Edinburgh in 2010, New York in 2013, and London in 2014. In 2015, he designed a work for Victoria Beckham’s store in London. His public works, such as The Scotsman Steps in Edinburgh, DON'T WORRY at St Peter's Church in Cologne, singing lifts at The Royal Festival Hall, London, and the spinning "MOTHERS" sign in Fort Worth, Texas, are freely accessible. Creed's works are held in museum collections worldwide, including at the Colleccion Jumex in Mexico City and The Lights Going On and Off at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Work No. 1000 consists of 1,000 hand prints made with broccoli, reflecting his comical, child-like approach. Work No. 975, Everything is Going to be Alright, was installed on the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art in November 2009; the phrase has appeared in other works, including a red neon text in New York’s Times Square (Work No. 225, 1999), a 30-metre-long version in Detroit (Work No. 790, 2007), and a 23-metre white neon version at the Rennie Museum in Vancouver (Work No. 851, 2008); a 46-metre multicoloured version was commissioned for Christchurch Art Gallery in 2017. In 2011, Creed was commissioned by Fruitmarket Gallery to create Work No. 1059, which clads 104 steps and landings in different marbles, described by Guardian critic Jonathan Jones as a "generous, modest masterpiece of contemporary public art." In 2012, he participated in Sketch, London’s long-term artist-conceived restaurant programme, creating Work No. 1343 where every piece of cutlery, glass, chair, and table was unique, and Work No. 1347, featuring 96 different types of marble in a herringbone pattern. In 2019, Work No. 2950: WHATEVER was installed on a building in Auckland, New Zealand, as a large multicoloured neon sign. Creed formed his first band, Owada, in 1994 with Adam McEwen and Keiko Owada, releasing their first CD, Nothing, in 1997 on David Cunningham's Piano label. Since 1999, he has not used the name Owada. In 2000, he released a solo recording titled I Can't Move under his own name with Art Metropole. A 2004 solo concert received a zero-star review in The Guardian. In 2010, he provided cover art for a Futuristic Retro Champions single and performed with his band, featuring Keiko Owada on bass, Genevieve Murphy on keyboards, Ben Kane on drums, and Anouchka Grose on steel guitar. Creed founded Telephone Records and released "Thinking/ Not Thinking" in early 2011, followed by "Where You Go" in 2012. In 2012, the Double AA Side single "Fuck Off" and "Die" was released on Moshi Moshi Records in May, ahead of the album Love To You, released in July, produced by David Cunningham, Martin Creed, and The Nice NIce Boys (Andrew Knowles of Johnny Marr & The Healers and Nick McCarthy of Franz Ferdinand). The Vinyl Factory produced a limited edition with hand-painted covers by Creed. "You're The One For Me" was released simultaneously with the album. In 2014, Mind Trap was released, featuring songs and instrumental pieces for orchestra, with Creed singing and playing instruments, supported by gospel singers Dee Alexander and Yvonne Gage and Andy Knowles on drums. Keiko Owada played bass on Gift Attack / Don't Won't. Co-produced by Martin and Andy Knowles, the album was recorded in London, Chicago, and the Czech Republic, with Nick McCarthy and Mark Ralph providing additional production. The Chicago tracks were recorded analog at Soma Studios. The Brno Philharmonic Orchestra, conducted by Mikel Toms, recorded three commissioned orchestral works: Work No. 955 for the Birmingham Symphony Orchestra, Work No. 994 for the Hiroshima Symphony Orchestra, and Work No. 1375 for the London Sinfonietta. All lyrics and music on the album are by Martin Creed, except "New Shutters," which is his arrangement of a traditional Neapolitan folk song. The album sleeve features Work No. 1674: Anouchka and was designed by Andy Knowles. Creed is well-regarded by Franz Ferdinand, who regularly attend his gigs and co-produced his Mind Trap album. In 2015, a new body of audiovisual work was released in response to the Syrian refugee crisis: the double A-side single “Let Them In / Border Control” was made available as free downloads on SoundCloud, accompanied by videos created by Creed. In July 2016, Creed released Thoughts Lined Up, including the singles "Understanding" and "Princess Taxi Girl," with accompanying videos. In a 2002 interview, Creed explained that he stopped making paintings because he didn’t like deciding what to paint, instead focusing on communicating with people, expressing himself, and wanting to be loved. He believes art is primarily emotional, driven by a desire to make something and connect with others. In 1996, Richard Long and Roger Ackling selected Creed for exhibition at EASTinternational. Since winning the Turner Prize, he has exhibited globally, including large survey shows at Trussardi Foundation, Milan ('I Like Things'), Bard College, New York ('Feelings'), and a touring exhibition from Ikon Gallery Birmingham to Hiroshima and Seoul. His first major survey, 'What's the point of it?', was held at the Hayward Gallery, London, in January 2014, featuring works such as Work No. 227, Work No. 293, and Work No. 1092 MOTHERS. In 2014, the Southbank Centre commissioned a new organ piece, Work No. 1815, performed alongside J.S. Bach’s works. His largest survey to date, The Back Door, took place at Park Avenue Armory, New York from June to August 2016, curated by Tom Eccles and Hans-Ulrich Obrist, featuring works from his over 20-year career. In 2017, he exhibited at Museum Voorlinden in the Netherlands titled Say Cheese, which included a wall of 1,000 broccoli prints in various colors, a room filled with blue balloons for walking through, and a room with metronomes ticking at different speeds. In 2019, the Centro Botín held an exhibition called Amigos from 6 April to 9 June, featuring new installations including one among trees surrounding the building. The Museum of Recent Art held an exhibition titled Thinking / Not Thinking from 12 February to 2 May 2019, showcasing several installations.
